newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Mir mishaps can't dim Russian space dream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mir mishaps can't dim Russian space dream.

text.p: We docked with the Mir space station smoothly enough last week, though a crewman had to make a spacewalk to repair asteroid damage before our Russian shuttle could return safely to Earth.

Our "mission" was pure fantasy, of course, a half-hour show aboard the quite genuine Buran (Blizzard) space shuttle, former flagship of the Soviet space fleet and now consigned to sit out its life as a fairground attraction in Moscow's Gorky Park.

Some might see the forlorn Buran and the ageing Mir, limping through space after a collision in June, as testaments to Soviet defeat in the Cold War space race, proof that "Upper Volta with rockets", as critics dubbed the USSR, no longer does rockets.
Yet Russian engineers and politicians will have none of it.
As President Boris Yeltsin's top defence adviser, Yuri Baturin, put it last week: "Rumours of the death of the Russian space programme are not only exaggerated but wrong."

True, the space industry has been in financial crisis since the collapse of communism -- the Russian Space Agency says state funding is at about 15 percent of Cold War levels and it has seen only 23 percent of 1997's modest $385 million budget.

True, there has been a brain drain of talent. True, Mir's electrical system needs risky repairs next month if the West is to keep pumping money into it. True, Russia's Mars-96 probe ended up in the ocean last year. And true, Buran, a dead ringer for the U.S. shuttle, flew for the first and last time in 1988.
RUSSIA STILL LEADS IN SOME SPACE TECHNOLOGIES
Yet Russia, proud of the tradition that built the first satellite and sent the first man into space, still has a lead in some technologies, notably space stations and launch rockets.
In Soviet times, that expertise was won at the expense of the consumer economy -- hence the "Upper Volta" jibe. Now it is one of the more promising areas for Russian commercial success.

Mir (Peace), whose original five-year lifespan should have ended with the Soviet Union in 1991, has been turned into a cash cow for the Russian space industry, bringing in hundreds of millions of dollars from NASA and other western space agencies.
The world's only manned orbital station, it has been a valuable laboratory for experiments requiring zero gravity and a testbed for the $50-billion international space station Alpha.
Russia, helped by $190 million from aircraft maker Boeing, is due to launch the first Alpha component in June next year.

Some U.S. politicians, exasperated by delays caused by Russian budget problems and alarmed when a cargo craft crashed into Mir on June 25 while NASA physicist Michael Foale was on board, want drastic cuts in cooperation with the Russians.

President Bill Clinton's top science adviser, Jack Gibbons, said last week that the U.S. may not send its next astronaut, Wendy Lawrence, to Mir in September if the two cosmonauts who blast off on August 5 fail to restore power to its laboratories.
But NASA experts stress that Russia is bringing both unique expertise and low-cost facilities to the joint space programmes.

Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev, who plans to ask the Kremlin for some $15 to $20 million to repair Mir, admits to worries about Congressional pressure on NASA. But he hopes for an end to delays in Russian state funding for the Alpha project.
The indications are that, for all its budgetary problems, the government is not ready to drop one of the few industries in which Russia has real competitive advantages.
"If we dump space now, we will lag behind in this field forever," said Baturin, otherwise the Kremlin's chief hatchet man on the defence budget, as he defended investment in space.
REFORMERS BACK SPACE SECTOR
Powerful reformers like First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais have also thrown their weight behind the space sector as one which can pay its way on a competitive world market.
Koptev has forecast that Russia will earn more than $600 million from space this year -- though that may depend partly on fixing Mir -- up from $471 million in 1996 and just $20 million in 1992.
The Khrunichev design group and Energia rocket maker are teamed with Lockheed Martin of the U.S. to market launch services to satellite owners. Contracts to date top $1 billion.
Energia is also working with Boeing and Norwegian and Ukrainian firms on the Sea Launch project, offering cheap launches near the Equator from a moveable converted oil rig.
At the Paris Air Show last month, Moscow's Energomash, the pioneer of Soviet rocketry, signed a $1 billion contract with Lockheed to supply 101 engines for Lockheed's Atlas rockets.
And a host of smaller ventures is bubbling away, including in satellite manufacture.

Western firms complain that the process of cooperating with their former Cold War rivals can be frustrating. In computing and electronics, some say Russia may be 15 or 20 years behind the West. But, generally, the space industry is developing.
"I see progress month by month," said Alain Fournier-Sicre, the European Space Agency's representative in Moscow. "There are weaknesses. But this is an industry with real possibilities."
LESSONS FOR THE FUTURE
In contrast to the plant closures that have characterised much of post-Soviet industry, Russia has opened a new launch site at Svobodny in the Far East and plans to reopen another.

Even the embarrassments of Mir's recent calamities, from overflowing toilets and mysterious leaks to a serious fire, the collision and the present station commander's stress-induced heart trouble, are put in a positive light by many experts.
"We have gone through some very dark times but...we have learnt valuable lessons for the future," Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev said in a radio link-up from space last week.
Baturin boasted that Russia would have "unique technology" -- once it had figured out how to patch up the station.
"I feel we're getting extremely valuable lessons," said NASA's chief of Mir operations, Frank Culbertson.

Support for the space programme also appears to be still strong among a Russian public brought up on incessant Soviet space race propaganda and who tend to see the cosmos as one of the few remaining domains where Russia remains a superpower.

"Why are we interested in space? Because we're patriotic," said Natasha after a "ride" on the Gorky Park Buran with her children. "Our guys up there are just brilliant," daughter Lena added. "They'll sort everything out on Mir."
